## Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly permeating our daily lives. Whether in the workplace or during entertainment activities, our interaction with AI and AI systems are destined to become more frequent. In education, a wide range of AI technologies brings forth numerous opportu- nities and challenges to navigate and explore. Preliminary research indicates that AI tools, such as ChatGPT, could be beneficial for improving knowledge acquisition and refining students’ writing skills and tasks (Chatterjee & Dethlefs, [2023;](#data-availability-statement) Terwiesch, 2023). Despite AI already being utilized in diverse industries (Ahuja, [2019;](#data-availability-statement) Veloso et al., 2021), the exploration of AI integration into classrooms and its influence on students’ learning is still at the beginning (Hwang & Chang, 2021).

AI offers numerous benefits if integrated properly into the classroom activities. Emphasizing the importance of equipping teachers with the essential skills to effectively integrate artificial intelligence tools (Ayanwale et  al., [2022)](#data-availability-statement). For example, teachers can utilize AI to personalize the learning process, matching it to students’ needs and learning styles, simplify administrative tasks, save time to focus more on the creative and critical aspects of teaching, and provide

JOURNAL OF DIGITAL LEARNING IN TEACHER EDUCATION 143

real-time feedback on student performance. AI can also help teachers facilitate adaptive learn- ing, granting students access to a wide range of educational resources and promoting inclusive education through accessibility features (Kim & Kwon, 2023; Kong & Abelson, 2022). Furthermore, AI is capable of fostering continuous improvement in the educational system by analyzing data to inform data-driven decisions (Rasul, 2023). Therefore, AI is a promising technology to be integrated into classroom activities. However, educators voice concerns about the potential drawbacks of incorporating specific AI tools into students’ learning experiences. There are concerns that certain AI tools with human-like responses may lead students to misuse them for exam-solving and essay writing, potentially hindering the development of students cognitive and mental capabilities (Zhai, 2022). Therefore, teachers today are required to understand what AI is, what it can do inside and outside the classroom, and engage with AI technologies in a self-determined manner. These set of skills, including understanding, utilizing, and integrating various AI technologies to enhance teaching methods, facilitate stu- dent learning, and improve overall educational outcomes, is commonly referred to as AI literacy among teachers (Carolus et  al., [2023)](#data-availability-statement).

AI literacy among teachers today is essential, some of the key reasons include: (**a)** Preparing students for the future, AI is rapidly becoming an integral part of various indus- tries and sectors. teachers can equip students with the necessary knowledge and skills to thrive in this technology-driven world (Chen et al., [2020)](#data-availability-statement). (**b)** Addressing ethical and social implications, AI technologies raise ethical concerns like privacy issues. Teachers can guide students on using AI responsibly and understand its social impact (Saylam et al., 2023). (**c)** Enhancing educational methods, AI has the potential to transform education by offering personalized learning experiences and automating administrative tasks. Teachers need to know AI to leverage its benefits effectively in the classroom (Holmes et  al., 2019; Kamalov et  al., 2023).

## The present study

### _Study problem_

AI literacy among teachers is relatively a new research domain, and research on AI integra- tion is still beginning (Southworth et  al., 2023). However, AI literacy is crucial for teachers to prepare students for the future, understand the impact of AI, develop classroom-ready AI resources, and save time. AI literacy is often viewed as an extension or specialization of ICT literacy for several reasons, this perspective is prevalent in the “government-sanctioned AI curricula” identified by UNESCO in its recent mapping exercise (Miao & Shiohira, 2022). However, AI is considered qualitatively different from typical ICT technologies as AI operates autonomously and can adapt based on contextual learning (Holmes et  al., 2019). Given the educational benefits and obstacles of AI and the major changes it brings to the classroom, improving AI literacy skills among teachers is vital for improving the integration process. Professional development is necessary to equip teachers with necessary skills to tackle the obstacles and increase the benefits of this new technology. Evaluating teachers’ AI literacy skills during professional development is crucial for successfully incorporating this new tech- nology into classroom activities. Policymakers could also take informed decisions to nurture AI integration based on well-defined professional development and assessment processes.

### _Purpose of the study_

This study aims to assess AI literacy among a group of preservice-teachers, and investigate the effectiveness of a proposed AI literacy professional development program **(PDP)** in developing their AI literacy skills.

144 B. YOUNIS

### _Research questions_

In this research, we sought to answer the following two research questions:

- What are AI literacy levels among a group of pre-services teachers before participating in the AI literacy PDP?
- To what extent do preservice teachers acquire AI literacy skills when participating in an AI literacy PDP?

## Literature review and theoretical framework

AI literacy is often viewed as an extension or specialization of ICT literacy (Miao & Shiohira, 2022). However, AI is considered qualitatively different from typical digital technologies as it operates autonomously and can adapt based on contextual learning (Holmes et  al., 2019). Therefore, AI literacy should go beyond just understanding the technical components and include an understanding of AI impact on people, such as human cognition, privacy, and agency. This broader approach is advocated by UNICEF (2021).

### _Competencies for AI education_

Based on Touretzky et  al. (2019) work, researchers have been actively identifying essential abil- ities and skill sets for teachers and students in K-12 AI education. The identified skill sets can be categorized into competencies for students and competencies for teachers. Notably, teachers need to regularly update their competencies to integrate AI effectively into the curriculum. This includes understanding AI concepts, principles, and being proficient in using AI-based tools to enhance students’ skills (Kong & Abelson, 2022; Su et al., 2022). In this notion, Ng et al. (2021) conducted a systematic literature of 30 peer-reviewed articles to establish a theoretical foundation for defining, teaching, and evaluating AI literacy. This work proposed four aspects: gaining knowledge and understanding of AI, using and applying AI, evaluating and creating AI, and reflecting on AI ethics. Ng et  al. (2023) further suggested a set of teachers’ AI competencies such as: using basic applications, managing information, creating learning content, and connecting with students _via_ technology.

### _AI literacy TPACK framework_

To organize these competencies systematically, researchers commonly employed the TPACK framework. This framework categorizes teacher-focused competencies into three areas: Content Knowledge (CK), Pedagogical Knowledge (PK), and Technical Knowledge (TK).

#### _AI-content knowledge_

Teachers need a deep understanding of their subject matter, but now, it should also encompass knowledge of AI’s relevance and applications within their specific content areas. This is crucial for effectively integrating AI into teaching practices and ensuring that students are equipped with the necessary skills to navigate the AI-driven world. The growing impact of AI on humanity makes AI literacy extremely important, not only for students but also for teachers. Teachers need to know how to use AI technologies explicitly in their teaching, as well as consider ethical issues. AI literacy involves the critical skills individuals need to learn and live in the digital world with the help of AI-based technologies. It includes four dimensions: Knowing and Understanding AI, Applying AI, Evaluating AI Application and AI Ethics (Lérias et  al., 2024).

JOURNAL OF DIGITAL LEARNING IN TEACHER EDUCATION 145

#### _AI-pedagogical knowledge_

Pedagogical Knowledge (PK) refers to the essential understanding teachers need to have regarding effective teaching strategies. However, in the current landscape, it is imperative for educators to also be equipped with pedagogical techniques specifically tailored to seamlessly integrate AI technologies into their instructional methods. This involves not only having a solid foundation in traditional teaching practices but also the ability to adapt and innovate teaching approaches to effectively incorporate AI tools and resources in the classroom. By enhancing their PK with AI-specific pedagogical knowledge, teachers can optimize the use of AI technologies to enhance student learning experiences and outcomes (Yue et  al., 2024).

#### _AI-technological knowledge_

Technological Knowledge (TK) is a crucial component of the TPACK framework, and in the context of AI education, it is essential for teachers to develop proficiency with AI tools and platforms relevant to educational contexts. This involves understanding the functionalities and limitations of various AI technologies that can be integrated into teaching practices (Celik, [2023;](#data-availability-statement) Ng et al., 2023). Teachers should focus on gaining hands-on experience with AI tools and plat- forms, such as intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, and AI-powered learning analytics platforms (Celik, [2023;](#data-availability-statement) Ng et  al., 2023). By understanding the capabilities and constraints of these tech- nologies, teachers can make informed decisions about which tools to use in their classrooms and how to effectively integrate them into their teaching methods (Velander et  al., 2023) ([Figure 1)](#ai-pedagogical-knowledge).

The interconnections between these types of knowledge lead to the emergence of three more constructs: technological content knowledge (TCK), technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK), and pedagogical content knowledge (PCK).

#### _AI-technological content knowledge (TCK)_

This knowledge involves understanding the relationship between technology and the content being taught, with a focus on how AI can be used to enhance the learning experience. In the context of AI education, TCK is crucial for teachers to effectively integrate AI technologies into their teaching practices (Yue et  al., 2024). Teachers need to understand how AI can be used to simulate or model the concepts being taught, as well as how AI can support the development of critical thinking, problem-solving, and creativity skills. This involves knowledge of AI appli- cations in various subjects, such as language, mathematics, science, and social studies, and how AI can be used to create personalized learning experiences for students (Yue et  al., 2024). Moreover, TCK for AI education requires teachers to be aware of the ethical considerations surrounding the use of AI in education, such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and transparency. By developing a strong TCK in AI, teachers can navigate these complex issues and ensure that the use of AI technologies in their classrooms is ethical, equitable, and effective (Valender, et al, 2024).

#### _AI-technological pedagogical knowledge_

Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK) in AI education is crucial for teachers to effectively integrate AI-based tools into their teaching practices. Research indicates that TPK plays a sig- nificant role in the integration of AI technologies in education, emphasizing the importance of teachers’ knowledge in utilizing AI tools effectively (Celik, [2023;](#data-availability-statement) Ning et  al., 2024). Teachers need to possess AI-specific technological and pedagogical knowledge to integrate AI into their teaching methods and consider the ethical implications of AI-based decisions (Celik, [2023)](#data-availability-statement). The TPK framework has been extended to include ethical aspects, highlighting the need for teachers to assess the ethical implications when using AI-based tools (Celik, [2023;](#data-availability-statement) Ning et  al., 2024). Additionally, the AI-TPACK framework emphasizes the importance of TPK in integrating AI technologies, showcasing the dynamic understanding required to design effective teaching strat- egies and activities using AI tools (Ning et al., 2024). Overall, TPK is a critical component that guides teachers in the pedagogical and ethical use of AI-based tools in education, ensuring that they can leverage AI technologies to enhance student learning experiences effectively.

#### _AI-pedagogical content knowledge (PCK)_

To effectively integrate AI in the classroom, teachers need to develop Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) specific to AI. PCK refers to the specialized knowledge that teachers use to transform their content knowledge into forms that are comprehensible to students (Asad et al., [2023;](#data-availability-statement) Lorenz & Romeike, 2023). Key aspects of AI-related PCK for teachers include: (a) Understanding how AI can be used to enhance teaching and learning (Asad et  al., [2023)](#data-availability-statement). This includes knowledge of AI-powered tools that can provide personalized feedback, generate learning materials, and enable adaptive learning experiences. (b) Knowing how to adapt existing teaching strategies to effectively incorporate AI (Lorenz & Romeike, 2023). Teachers need to plan how to integrate AI into their lessons and assess its impact on student learning and engagement. 

1. Developing awareness of the technical aspects of AI systems at a high level (Lorenz & Romeike, 2023). This involves understanding AI concepts like machine learning, neural networks, and data processing, without needing to be an AI expert. (d) Recognizing the strengths, lim- itations, and potential issues with using AI in education (Lorenz & Romeike, 2023). Teachers should be able to critically evaluate AI tools and make informed decisions about their use. (e) Communicating effectively with students about AI and its applications (Park et  al., 2023). This requires the ability to explain AI concepts in an age-appropriate manner and address ethical considerations like bias and privacy. (f) Designing learning activities that leverage AI to enhance understanding of subject matter (Asad et  al., [2023;](#data-availability-statement) Park et  al., 2023). For example, using AI-powered simulations to visualize complex scientific concepts. (g) Assessing student learning in the context of AI-integrated lessons (Lorenz & Romeike, 2023). This involves adapting 

JOURNAL OF DIGITAL LEARNING IN TEACHER EDUCATION 147

assessment methods to account for the use of AI tools and ensuring that students are demon- strating the intended learning outcomes. By developing this specialized PCK, teachers can harness the potential of AI to create more engaging, personalized, and effective learning experiences for their students. Therefore, it becomes essential for teachers to acquire essential TPACK knowledge and familiarize themselves with the pedagogies that form the foundation of a given AI system. Moreover, they should understand how the AI system address the learning objectives and comprehend the ethical considerations involved. Furthermore, assessment plays a crucial role in gauging students’ progress in AI-integrated learning. This assessment must be sensitive to the diverse cognitive domains. Rather than solely assessing fundamental AI comprehension, it should also evaluate higher-order thinking skills like collaboration, communication, and creativity.

### _DigCompEdu framework_

DigCompEdu is a framework developed by the European Commission’s Joint Research Center (JRC) that defines the digital competences needed by educators to enhance and innovate edu- cation through the effective use of digital technologies (Ovcharuk, 2020).

The key aspects of DigCompEdu are: professional engagement, digital resources, teaching and learning, assessment, empowering learners, and facilitating learners’ digital competence. Each area contains several competences, with a total of 22 competences across the framework (Feng & Xue, [2023)](#data-availability-statement). For example, under “Digital Resources,” the competences include “Selecting,” “Creating and Modifying,” and “Managing, Protecting and Sharing” digital resources. The frame- work aims to support educators in developing their digital competences to effectively integrate digital technologies into teaching and learning. It provides a common reference point for pro- fessional development and training (Feng & Xue, [2023)](#data-availability-statement). In summary, DigCompEdu is a com- prehensive framework that defines the key digital competences needed by educators, provides a structure for professional development, and is supported by a self-assessment tool to help teachers identify their strengths and areas for improvement.

Based on the AI literacy TPACK model and the DigCompEdu framework, Ng et  al. (2023) proposed a new framework that extends the previous models to incorporate AI and meet the latest learning standards. This new framework emphasizes that AI competencies should involve more than just technological skills; it should also include a comprehensive understanding of non-technical, critical, and complex competencies. These competencies enable young people to ethically, safely, and wisely interact with AI technologies. The framework aims to address the broader aspects of AI education and its ethical implications ([Figure 2)](#digcompedu-framework).

### _AI literacy competencies for teachers_

This study implemented a PDP based on the Instructional Design Framework for AI Literacy. This proposed PDP provides teachers with guidance on utilizing the ADDIE model phases and skills to tackle the educational challenges of effective integration of AI in classroom activities. The ultimate goal is to identify successful solutions for AI integration process. The main goal for the PDP is to improve teachers’ ability to integrate AI technology in classroom activities. This integration helps teachers prepare their students for the AI-dominated future and provide them with vital skills for the upcoming job market by understanding and mastering these AI literacy attitudes, knowledge, and skills. ## Methodology

### _Research design and context_

### This study employed a pretest post-test quasi-experimental design to investigate the effectiveness of the AI Literacy Professional Development Program (PDP), following the recommendations of Shadish et al. (2002) for conducting rigorous quasi-experimental research. Data were collected using a pretest post-test design, as suggested by Dimitrov and Rumrill ([2003)](#data-availability-statement), who emphasized the importance of this approach in evaluating educational interventions. The participants were 37 undergraduate students from Palestine Technical University Kadoorie and Hebron University, who volunteered for the PDP during the second semester of the 2023–2024 academic year. These participants were pre-service teachers in the final stages of their Bachelor’s degree programs.

The AI literacy Professional Development Program (PDP) consisted of a series of training modules designed to enhance the participants’ ability to integrate AI technologies in educational settings. The program began with an introduction to AI and ChatGPT, providing a foundational understanding of AI technology. The participants then engaged in hands-on experiences with ChatGPT, aligning with the principles of experiential learning. The program also guided the participants in identifying use cases for ChatGPT in teaching. The participants were then trained in designing lessons that incorporate ChatGPT, addressing the challenges and limitations of the technology, and promoting responsible AI usage. The PDP consisted of 24 training hours divided into three sessions, aligning with the recommendations of Desimone ([2009)](#data-availability-statement), who suggested that effective professional development should be sustained over time and include multiple sessions.

## _The participants_

The target population of this study consisted of a fourth year undergraduate students from two universities. Table 2 presents demographic data of the participants.

### _The instrument_

A self-reporting confidence questionaries’ was developed by the researcher to evaluate AI literacy. questionnaire was crafted based on a thorough review of relevant literature, focusing on the AI Literacy TPACK Framework and the Instructional Design Framework for AI Literacy (Ng et al., 2021, 2023; Olari & Romeike, 2021).

### _Questionaries’ structure_

The questionnaire comprised three sections: (1) Introduction: This section introduced the study’s objectives and subject matter. (2) Demographic Data: The second section collected demographic information such as gender and specialty area of the participants. (3) Assessment Factors: The third

The participants rated their responses using a five-point Likert scale to indicate their level of agreement.

150 B. YOUNIS

#### _Administration_

The questionnaire was administered to the participants before starting the AI literacy Professional Development Program (PDP) and then repeated three days after the conclusion of the final session of the PDP. This approach allowed for a comprehensive assessment of participants’ AI literacy levels and any changes resulting from the PDP.

### _Validity and reliability of the instrument_

#### _Validity assessment_

To assess the validity of the AI literacy questionnaire, the instrument was presented to a panel of 7 experts. These experts held graduate degrees and possessed extensive experience in instruc- tional design. The experts evaluated the accuracy, clarity, and appropriateness of the AI literacy scale. Based on the experts’ feedback, a final version of the scale, consisting of 42 items, was developed.

#### _Reliability assessment_

To determine the internal consistency reliability of the AI literacy scale, Cronbach’s Alpha was calculated. The scale scored a Cronbach’s Alpha of .88, which is an accepted value for the pur- poses of this study (Taber, 2018). This high reliability coefficient indicates that the items within the scale are closely related and measure the same construct consistently.

## The use of expert evaluation and Cronbach’s Alpha provides strong evidence for the validity and reliability of the AI literacy questionnaire. The expert review process ensures that the scale accurately measures the intended constructs, while the high internal consistency reliability sug- gests that the scale produces stable and consistent results across different administrations.

# Results

The Shapiro-Wilk test was conducted to assess normality. The _p_value for the post-test AI literacy and pretest AI literacy were 0.103 and 0.059, respectively, indicating that the data are normally distributed.

Arithmetic mean score was obtained from the participants’ responses on the AI literacy scale before participating in the PDP as follows (Table 3).

The arithmetic mean score of AI literacy among the participants before joining the AI literacy PDP was 2.294. This means the participants had low level of AI literacy skills. However, the highest mean on AI literacy factors was given to teachers’ attitudes toward AI with 2.942 score, which mean that they had moderate level of attitudes toward AI. Otherwise, the lowest mean on the AI literacy factors was given to understanding AI and computational thinking concepts

An independent sample t-test was also conducted to assess whether a significant difference in AI literacy scores exist based on gender before participating in the AI literacy PDP.

As shown in Table 4, the mean AI literacy score for males was 2.2764 (SD = .4832), while for females it was 2.3120 (SD = .3583). The t-test value of −2.253 with a _p_value greater than .05 suggests that the difference in AI literacy scores between males and females was not statis- tically significant before the PDP intervention.

One Way Analysis of Variance was also conducted to assess whether a significant difference in AI literacy scores exist based on specialty area before participating in the AI literacy PDP (Table 5).

Table 6 illustrates the mean AI literacy scores by specialty area before the Professional Development Program (PDP). The data shows significant differences in AI literacy skills among participants based on their specialty areas. To determine the direction of these differences, the LSD (Least Significant Difference) test was applied.

By analyzing Table 7 results, it is evident that there are significant variations in AI literacy skills among participants based on their specialty areas. LSD test results shows that the partic- ipants with computer science specialty area had the highest AI literacy with a moderate score of 2.863. Otherwise, pre-service teachers in religions specialty had the lowest AI literacy with a weak score of 1.771.t-test was also conducted to assess whether a significant difference in AI literacy scores exists based on participating in the AI literacy PDP (Table 8).

The t-test results indicate that there was a significant difference in AI literacy scores before and after participating in the AI literacy PDP. The mean AI literacy score increased from 2.294 (SD = 0.4181) before participating in the PDP to 4.325 (SD = 0.3781) after participating in the PDP. This difference was statistically significant, t(36) = −21.913, _p_ \< .05. These findings suggest that the AI literacy PDP was effective in improving the participants’ understanding and knowl- edge of AI concepts and technologies (Table 9).

The general arithmetic mean score of AI literacy among the participants after joining the AI literacy PDP was 4.325, This means that the participants had high levels of AI literacy skills. All the factors received high score levels ranged from 3.432 score given to understanding AI and computational thinking concepts to 4.471 score given to teachers’ attitudes toward AI.

An independent sample t-test was also conducted to assess whether a significant difference in AI literacy scores exist based on gender after participating in the AI literacy PDP (Table 10).

The independent sample t-test results indicate that there was no significant difference in AI literacy scores between male and female participants after completing the AI literacy PDP. The mean AI literacy score for males was 4.293 (SD = 0.3839), while for females it was 4.355 (SD = 0.3805). This difference was not statistically significant, t(35) = −0.495, _p_ \> .05. These findings suggest that the AI literacy PDP was equally effective in improving AI literacy among both male and female participants. The lack of a significant gender difference implies that the PDP content and delivery were inclusive and accessible to participants regardless of their gender.

One Way Analysis of Variance was also conducted to assess whether a significant difference in AI literacy scores exist based on specialty area after participating in the AI literacy PDP (Tables 11 and 12).

The One-Way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) results indicate that there was no significant difference in AI literacy scores based on specialty area after participating in the AI literacy Partnership PDP. The ANOVA test showed that the F-value was 1.256 with a _p_value of 0.308, indicating that there was no statistically significant difference in AI literacy scores among dif- ferent specialty areas. This suggests that the AI literacy curriculum implemented through the

## Discussion

This study investigated the effect of a PDP in improving AI literacy skills among a group of preservice teachers. The empirical findings showed that the mean score of AI literacy among the participants changed from 2.294 to 4.325 (t (37) = −21.913, _p_\< 0.05) after participating in the PDP. Therefore, the PDP was effective strategy in developing the AI literacy skills, this finding was supported by Nazaretsky et  al. (2022) and Frimpong ([2022)](#data-availability-statement). The AI literacy level was high (_m_ = 4.325) among the participants after finishing the PDP, even though the AI literacy level was low (_m_= 2.294) before joining the PDP program. AI literacy is crucial for teachers to understand AI concepts, ethics, and applications for social good, influencing their behavioral intentions to learn AI (Du et  al., [2024;](#data-availability-statement) Casal-Otero et  al., [2023)](#data-availability-statement). Previous research called for improving AI literacy training to enhance teachers’ professional learning in AI to leverage its benefits in education (Batanero et  al., [2019;](#data-availability-statement) Holstein et  al., 2018).

The results also indicated that pre-service teachers have pleasing attitudes toward the use of AI before participating in the PDP (_m_= 2.942) which increased to (_m_ = 4.471) after completing the program. Previous research showed that attitudes of US teachers toward educational tech- nologies, including those with AI, are generally positive (Cojean et  al., [2023;](#data-availability-statement) Eyüp & Kayhan, [2023)](#data-availability-statement). This suggests that the PDP was effective in enhancing pre-service teachers’ attitudes and perceptions of AI’s potential in education. The training likely provided them with a better understanding of AI concepts, applications, and benefits, leading to more positive attitudes (Pokrivcakova, 2024). Improving pre-service teachers’ AI literacy through PDPs is crucial, as many lack adequate knowledge and skills in this area (Pokrivcakova, 2024). By addressing this gap, PDPs can help future teachers effectively integrate AI into their teaching practices and leverage its benefits for student learning (Lee et  al., 2024; Pokrivcakova, 2024). The findings highlight the importance of providing pre-service teachers with opportunities to learn about AI through well-designed PDPs. Such programs should focus on developing a solid understanding of AI principles, ethics, and practical applications in educational settings (Lee et  al., 2024; Pokrivcakova, 2024).

The empirical finding of this research showed that the AI literacy factor “understand AI and computational thinking concepts” received the least mean score both before joining the PDP (_m_= 3.432), and after finishing the PDP (_m_= 1.859). The challenge in understanding AI and computational thinking concepts for preservice teachers could stem from factors such as lack 

154 B. YOUNIS

of familiarity, fear of replacement, ethical considerations (Kim & Kim, 2022). Even though the preservice teachers have limited understanding of AI and computational thinking concepts. They perceive it as an opportunity for education, and need support to be efficient and effective in their work practice (Chounta et  al., [2021)](#data-availability-statement).

This study found that no significant difference exists between male and female preservice teachers on AI literacy skills both before and after participating in the AI literacy PDP. Literature on AI literacy has thus far provided conflicting results about the impact of gender. For example, female teachers may be more apprehensive about utilizing AI-based applications in their teaching and learning processes than male teachers (Zhang et  al., 2023).

This study found a significant difference in AI literacy among the participants before joining the PDP based on specialty area in favor of computer science education, science education, and math education specialty areas. Previous studies on AI literacy skills revealed that STEM teachers positively experienced AI as a source for superior scaffolding in scientific writing, indicating a positive perception of AI utilization in specific educational domains (Kim & Kim, 2022). However, there are challenges related to teachers’ perceptions of AI uses and limitations of technology availability in their classrooms, which highlights the need to address varying attitudes toward AI integration across different specialty areas (Chounta et  al., [2021)](#data-availability-statement). This finding underscores the importance of considering participants’ specialty areas when designing AI literacy training programs. Tailoring such programs to address the specific needs and knowledge levels of indi- viduals from different specialty areas can enhance the effectiveness of AI education initiatives and better prepare teachers to integrate AI concepts into their teaching practices

After finishing the PDP, the participants got high mean scores on AI literacy factors. Their mean scores ranged from _m_ = 3.432 to _m_ = 4.471 with no significant differences based on specialty area of the participants. The effectiveness of the PDP in developing AI literacy among teachers suggests that it can be a valuable tool for enhancing their understanding and knowledge of AI concepts and applications. This finding indicates that teachers can acquire the necessary skills and knowledge to integrate AI into their teaching practices through well-designed professional development programs. Most of the educational literature supports the idea that technology training is an important component to help teachers gain positive attitudes toward technology and achieve technology literacy (Zhao & Bryant, 2006). This training should move beyond exposure to basic computational thinking skills into deeper, meaningful, and exemplar activities that show teachers how to integrate the AI technologies into the curriculum and the classroom as given in this PDP (Baylor & Ritchie, [2002;](#data-availability-statement) Masoud, 2019; Zhao & Bryant, 2006).

### _Implications and recommendations_

In conclusion, the present study has found that the suggested PDP is effective learning environment for promoting AI literacy. This finding provides educators, administrators, and stakeholders with research results that support integrating AI in teachers’ preparation programs. By incorporating AI into the TPACK framework, the PDP helps teachers develop a more comprehensive understanding of the interactions between technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge. This expanded TPACK framework, known as AI-TPACK, enables teachers to make more informed decisions about integrating AI technologies into their teaching methods and lesson plans. The development of AI-TPACK among teachers can facilitate collaboration and knowledge sharing within and across educational institutions. Teachers can work together to design and implement AI-integrated learning activities, share best practices, and support each other in their professional growth. It will also enable curriculum designers to integrate AI in school curriculum combined with professional development that supports active involvement of teachers in the integration process.

This study found a significant difference in AI literacy among the participants before joining the PDP based on specialty area in favor of computer science, math, and science specialty areas. Tailoring professional development to address the specific needs and knowledge levels of indi- viduals from different specialty areas can enhance the effectiveness of AI education initiatives 

JOURNAL OF DIGITAL LEARNING IN TEACHER EDUCATION 155

and better prepare teachers to integrate AI concepts into their teaching practices. Given the research results, it is recommended that teachers should be supported to integrate AI in class- room activities. AI technological tools should be included in pre- service and in-service training programs. Further AI tools combined with other professional development strategies should be researched among teachers from different subjects to enable generalizing the finding of this research and increasing it is validity. However, it is important to note that the study did not include a control group, so it is unclear whether the observed improvement was solely due to the PDP or if other factors may have contributed to the increase in AI literacy scores. Additionally, the small sample size (_N_= 37) may limit the generalizability of the results.
